q: What is a Transformer?
short: A sequence model built from stacked layers of multi-head self-attention and position-wise feed-forward networks, each with residual connections and layer normalisation, with no recurrence.
detail: Positional encodings supply order; encoder, decoder or both.
mistakes: Saying it is 'just attention' and forgetting the FFN.

q: Why did Transformers replace RNNs?
short: Full parallelism over positions during training, O(1) path between any two tokens (no vanishing over time), and better scaling with data and compute.
detail: Cost: O(n²) attention memory.
follow: When might RNNs/SSMs still be preferable?

q: Encoder-only vs decoder-only vs encoder–decoder?
short: Encoder-only: bidirectional, understanding (BERT). Decoder-only: causal, generation (GPT). Encoder–decoder: bidirectional encoder + causal decoder with cross-attention, transformation (T5, BART).
detail: Choice is about attention pattern and task.

q: What does the position-wise feed-forward network do?
short: Applies the same two-layer MLP (d → 4d → d, ReLU/GELU) to each token independently, adding non-linear processing after attention mixes tokens.
detail: Holds ≈2/3 of a layer's parameters.

q: Why residual connections and layer norm in Transformers?
short: Residuals give gradient highways and let layers learn refinements; layer norm stabilises activations per token. Together they make deep stacks trainable.
detail: Pre-norm vs post-norm placement.

q: What is cross-attention in the decoder?
short: An attention sub-layer whose queries come from the decoder and keys/values from the encoder output, letting each target position look at the source.
detail: No causal mask over the source.

q: How is BERT pretrained?
short: Masked language modelling: mask ≈15% of tokens and predict them from both sides (original BERT also used next-sentence prediction).
detail: 80/10/10 mask/random/keep.

q: How does a Vision Transformer process an image?
short: Split into P×P patches (196 for 224², P = 16), flatten and project each to d, prepend [CLS], add learned positions, run a Transformer encoder, classify from [CLS].
detail: Needs large pretraining.
follow: ViT vs CNN on small data?

q: What learning rate and epochs for fine-tuning BERT?
short: Small: 2e-5–5e-5 with AdamW, weight decay ≈0.01, 2–5 epochs, warmup, gradient clipping 1.0.
detail: Large rates destroy pretrained features (catastrophic forgetting).
follow: How to choose between full fine-tuning and LoRA?

q: What is LoRA?
short: Freeze pretrained weights and learn a low-rank update ΔW = BA (rank r ≪ d) for selected matrices: ~0.1–1% trainable parameters, similar accuracy, mergeable at inference.
detail: B initialised to zero.
example: BERT-base r = 8 on W_Q, W_V: ~295K params.

q: Derive the ≈12d² parameter count of an encoder layer.
short: Attention: W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O each d×d → 4d². FFN: d×4d + 4d×d = 8d². Plus 2 LayerNorms (4d) and biases. Total ≈ 12d².
detail: Decoder adds cross-attention 4d² → 16d².
follow: Where does an LLM's parameter budget go?
mistakes: Counting attention per head as d² each.

q: Why does the decoder need a causal mask during training?
short: Training processes all target positions in parallel with teacher forcing; without the mask each position could see the token it must predict, and the model would learn to copy.
detail: Mask sets future scores to −∞.
example: Verified: changing a later token doesn't change earlier outputs.
follow: Is the mask needed at inference?

q: Pre-norm vs post-norm?
short: Post-norm: LN(x + F(x)) (original), needs warmup, can be unstable deep. Pre-norm: x + F(LN(x)) (GPT-2 onwards), stable for deep stacks, needs a final LN.
detail: Slides use pre-norm.

q: What is the KV cache and why does it matter?
short: During generation, store each layer's keys and values for past tokens so each new token only computes its own Q, K, V and attends to cached ones: O(n) per step instead of recomputing O(n²).
detail: Memory grows with context length × layers × d.
follow: How do MQA/GQA reduce cache size?

q: ViT vs CNN: when to use which?
short: CNN: strong locality bias, data-efficient, good below ~100K images or limited compute. ViT: weak bias, global context, scales and transfers best with large pretraining; hybrids combine both.
detail: DeiT, Swin narrow the data gap.
example: Medical images with 5K samples → CNN or pretrained ViT fine-tuned.
follow: Why does ViT need more data?
mistakes: Saying ViT has no positional information.

q: You need to route 20K labelled support tickets to 15 teams. Which model and how?
short: Fine-tune an encoder (e.g. RoBERTa/DistilBERT) with a classification head: LR 2e-5, 3 epochs, stratified validation, macro-F1; consider LoRA if many tasks share a base.
detail: Check class imbalance; calibrate.
follow: When would a prompted LLM be better?

q: Explain greedy decoding, sampling and beam search.
short: Greedy: argmax each step (fast, repetitive). Sampling: draw from the distribution (temperature, top-k, top-p) for diversity. Beam search: keep k best partial sequences; good for translation.
detail: Beam search can be bland for open-ended text.
mistakes: Thinking beam search finds the global optimum.

q: Write a pre-norm encoder layer in NumPy.
short: Z1 = X + MHA(LN(X)); Z2 = Z1 + relu(LN(Z1) @ W1 + b1) @ W2 + b2, with MHA splitting d into heads and concatenating before W_O.
detail: See code ex1.
mistakes: Applying softmax over the wrong axis.

q: Why is attention O(n²) and how do long-context models cope?
short: Every query scores every key: n² scores per head per layer. Mitigations: FlashAttention (exact, IO-aware), sparse/sliding-window attention, linear attention, KV-cache compression, MQA/GQA, RoPE scaling for longer contexts.
detail: FFN cost is O(n d²) and dominates for short sequences.

q: MLM vs causal LM vs span corruption as pretraining objectives?
short: MLM (BERT): bidirectional context, great representations, not generative; ~15% of tokens give signal. Causal LM (GPT): every token is a target, natural generation, in-context learning. Span corruption (T5): encoder sees corrupted text, decoder generates spans; good for seq2seq.
detail: Prefix-LM and UL2 mix objectives.
example: GPT for chat, BERT for NER.
follow: Why did decoder-only win at scale?

q: Fine-tune a 7B LLM for a domain assistant on one 24 GB GPU.
short: QLoRA: 4-bit frozen base, LoRA adapters (r 8–64) on attention/FFN projections, gradient checkpointing, small batch with accumulation, LR ~1e-4–2e-4 for adapters, evaluate on held-out domain questions; consider retrieval instead if knowledge changes often.
detail: Full fine-tuning of 7B needs ~100+ GB with Adam states.

q: What does each Transformer component contribute, from an ablation perspective?
short: Attention: token mixing/context; FFN: per-token capacity (key–value memory); residuals: optimisation and identity paths; LayerNorm: stability; positions: order; multiple heads: diverse relations (many heads can be pruned post-training).
detail: Removing FFNs or residuals cripples training; removing positions makes it a bag of words.

q: Estimate BERT-base parameters.
short: 12 layers × ≈7.09M (12d² + biases + LN, d = 768) ≈ 85M, plus embeddings 30,522×768 + 512×768 ≈ 23.8M → ≈109M (published ≈110M).
detail: Token-type embeddings and pooler add a little.

q: How do mixture-of-experts Transformers work?
short: Replace the FFN with many expert FFNs and a router that sends each token to the top-k experts, so total parameters grow while compute per token stays roughly constant (sparse activation).
detail: Load-balancing losses keep experts used evenly.
mistakes: Assuming all experts run for every token.
